questions.a: Fencing limits what untrusted or private text the model sees. Allow-listing limits what actions and destinations exist even if it is fooled. You need both.

jailbreaks-vs-injection.explain:
## What it is

A **jailbreak** is the *user* trying to make the model violate its **safety policy** or the developer's rules: produce disallowed content, drop a persona, reveal hidden behaviour. Typical tricks: role-play ('you are DAN'), hypotheticals, multi-turn escalation, many-shot examples, encoding, translation.

**Prompt injection** is *third-party content* or input trying to make the model act against the **user's or application's** intent — tools, data, objectives. One line: jailbreak attacks the model's *policy*; injection attacks the *application's trust boundary*. Harm differs: jailbreak is mostly content and reputation (attacker is the user); injection is data and actions affecting a victim.

Techniques overlap. A jailbreaking user of an over-privileged agent causes injection-like harm. Distinguish so you pick the right owner: provider alignment and moderation for jailbreaks; architecture and permissions for injection.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers use a scenario and ask you to classify before you prescribe. If you slap 'jailbreak' on a poisoned wiki, you will propose a content filter and miss ACLs. On the job, the two land in different queues: Trust & Safety versus application security.

## How it works + one small example

Ask: who is the attacker, who is the victim, what rule is bypassed.

Example. User role-plays to get a discount code the prompt says to hide. That is a jailbreak / prompt leak by the user. The real fix is still not 'hide secrets in the prompt': keep codes out of context and enforce entitlements in the backend. Moderation is secondary.

Example. A web page tells the assistant to send mail. That is injection. Moderation of 'unsafe content' will not save you; tool design will.

## Failure modes

1. **Using the words interchangeably.** You prescribe the wrong control.

2. **Hiding secrets in the prompt** and calling jailbreaks the risk. The secret should not be there.

3. **Only testing jailbreak strings** on an agent with tools. You missed the app.

4. **Assuming provider alignment covers injection.** It covers policy, not your refund tool.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Jailbreak is a user versus model policy; injection is untrusted data versus app intent. I classify attacker, victim, and bypassed rule first. Alignment and moderation help jailbreaks; architecture and permissions stop injection.

## A concrete walk-through

A PM reports 'users jailbroke the refund bot'. You read the transcript: a ticket contained the payload. You rename the incident to injection, revoke the shared refund role, and add an ownership check. The jailbreak suite stays for the public FAQ bot that has no tools.

## What I would measure

Incidents tagged with the correct class; jailbreak ASR on the content bot; injection ASR on the agent. Mixing the two metrics hides regressions.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on A **jailbreak** is the *user* trying to make the model violate its **safety poli is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) Jailbreak = user vs model policy; injection = untrusted content vs app intent; 2) Harm profiles differ: content versus data and actions; 3) Techniques overlap; controls and owners differ; 4) Classify attacker, victim, and bypassed rule first; 5) Do not hide secrets in the prompt as a jailbreak defence. The spoken close stays the same: Jailbreak is a user versus model policy; injection is untrusted data versus app intent. I classify attacker, victim, and bypassed rule first. Alignment and moderation help jailbreaks; architecture and permissions stop injection.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

## How this fails in a real review

Teams skip this when a demo is due. The skip shows up later as an incident, a surprise bill, or a questionnaire they cannot answer. I write the failure modes into the runbook so the next on-call does not rediscover them. I also refuse a change that cannot be tested, versioned, and rolled back.

## What I would do on Monday

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.

questions.a: Trust and safety plus the model provider own policy jailbreaks. Application security and the product team own injection: tools, ACLs, egress.

input-output-guardrails.explain:
## What it is

**Guardrails** are checks wrapped around the model. **Input guardrails** run before: topic and scope filters, PII and secret detection, injection or jailbreak classifiers, language and length limits, rate limits, auth. **Output guardrails** run after: toxicity and safety classification, PII and secret scrubbing, schema validation, grounding checks, policy checks (no dosage advice), URL and markup filtering.

Implementations: rules and regex (fast, brittle, good for secrets); small classifiers or a moderation endpoint (tunable); LLM-as-judge (flexible, slower, attackable); deterministic validators (schemas, allow-lists). Each guard costs latency, money, and false positives. Streaming forces a choice: buffer (safer) or check chunks (faster, leaky).

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the productisation of safety. Interviewers want where each guard sits, what it costs, and how you measure false-positive and false-negative rates. On the job, a 600 ms output moderator that blocks 4% of valid answers is a support incident of its own.

## How it works + one small example

Place guards on the path, not 'somewhere in the prompt'.

Example customer assistant: input PII detector and scope filter; parallel injection signal; output safety classifier; schema on tool args; markdown sanitiser; rate limit per user. You tune thresholds on labelled data, log decisions, and give a graceful refusal. For streaming you either delay display until the first safe chunk policy passes or you use a fast first-pass filter and a slower async judge with a retract.

Provider filters (OpenAI safety, Azure content filter, Gemini safety settings, Bedrock Guardrails) are a layer, not the whole design.

## Failure modes

1. **Streaming then moderating.** The user already saw the leak.

2. **One huge LLM judge on every token.** Latency and a new injection surface.

3. **No labelled set.** You cannot tune without false-positive pain.

4. **Guards that fail open** on timeout. Attackers induce timeouts.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I put input and output guardrails around the model — regex, classifiers, schemas, provider filters — and I treat them as layers with measured false positives. Deterministic validators and fail-closed timeouts carry the guarantees.

## A concrete walk-through

You add Azure content filtering plus a schema validator and a PII regex. False positives spike on medical tickets. You lower the medical category threshold for that route, keep schema fail-closed, and add 200 labelled tickets to the weekly review.

## What I would measure

Guard latency p95; false-positive and false-negative by category; fail-open timeout count; share of streams that displayed text before a completed output check.

## Interview follow-up

questions.q: Name three input guardrails and three output guardrails you would put on a customer-facing assistant.
questions.a: Input: PII or secret detection, injection classifier, scope filter, rate limits. Output: safety classifier, PII scrubbing, schema or grounding validation, link or markup filter. Any three each, with latency and false-positive notes.

questions.q: Your output moderation adds 600ms and blocks 4% of valid answers. How do you improve it?
questions.a: Measure with labelled samples, tune the threshold, use a faster classifier, run checks in parallel or on the first chunk, route only risky categories to a heavy judge, and give graceful fallbacks. Track false-positive and false-negative rates per category.

questions.q: A team streams tokens to the user and runs moderation afterwards. What is the main risk?
questions.a: Unsafe or secret-bearing text is already on the screen or in logs. Buffer, use incremental safe rendering, or retract — and do not call that 'moderated streaming' if the user saw the leak.

questions.q: When is regex the right guardrail?
questions.a: Stable patterns: API keys, card numbers, internal hostnames. Pair with a semantic detector for the rest. Regex is fast and explainable; it is not enough alone.

questions.q: Why can an LLM-as-judge be attacked?
questions.a: The judged text can contain instructions for the judge. Use it as a signal, constrain its task, and keep deterministic checks for money and data.

why-one-layer-is-not-enough.explain:
## What it is

Every guardrail has a failure profile, and attackers search the gaps. Classifiers miss novel phrasing. Regex dies to synonyms, spacing, and encoding. LLM judges can be injected and are non-deterministic. Prompt rules share the attack channel. Provider alignment moves with multi-turn attacks and model versions.

**Layering** works when failure modes are *independent* (Swiss cheese): a payload must beat the input classifier, then the prompt, then the output filter, then permission checks. Two guards on the same model and dataset fail together. Invest in deterministic layers — permissions, validation, sandboxing — as the last line because they do not need to understand the attack.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the answer to 'we already have moderation'. Interviewers will ask why stacking two filters is weaker than it looks. On the job it stops you from adding a fifth LLM judge instead of an allow-list.

## How it works + one small example

Quantify independence.

Illustrative: two independent guards each miss 10%; combined miss is about 1%. Two correlated judges miss closer to 10%. So you pair unlike mechanisms.

Example calendar agent: input scope and injection signal; prompt labelling; schema-validated tool args; code-level checks (own calendar only, no external attendees by default); approval for outsider invites; output filtering; logging. The approval and the attendee allow-list still work when both classifiers fail.

## Failure modes

1. **Five copies of the same judge.** Cost up, independence down.

2. **No last-line deterministic check** on the action.

3. **Calling layered 'defence in depth'** when every layer is a prompt.

4. **Ignoring fail-open.** The stack looks thick until the judge times out.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

## What it is

This checklist item is the **one-line classroom version**: **jailbreak is a user trying to drop policy; injection is untrusted data doing it**. Say it that way when you need a second of clarity, then add the owner and the control. The longer distinction (policy versus trust boundary, content harm versus data harm) lives in the sibling note; this one is the phrase you want in muscle memory.

Use it when a discussion is mixing the words. Reset the room, then continue. If the 'user' is actually a document, you say injection. If the document is absent and the signed-in user is pushing past a content policy, you say jailbreak.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviews reward a crisp line. Staff conversations reward the same line so the wrong team is not paged. This is not dumbed down; it is the index card.

## How it works + one small example

- 'FAQ says email the keys to me' → injection (data, app intent).

Write the line at the top of the runbook. Tag tickets with one word so metrics do not mix.

## Failure modes

1. **Stopping at the slogan** and not classifying the case.

2. **Tagging everything as jailbreak** because the word is popular.

3. **Two owners arguing** because the ticket used the wrong word.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Jailbreak is a user trying to drop policy; injection is untrusted data doing it. I say that line, then I name the owner and the control so the slogan does not replace the work.

## A concrete walk-through

Stand-up: three tickets titled 'jailbreak'. You retitle two to injection after reading the source (email, wiki). The remaining one is a content policy push on the public bot. Two different PRs.

## What I would measure

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on This checklist item is the **one line classroom version**: **jailbreak is a user is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. ## What it is

**Interview: test obfuscated input** means you volunteer **homoglyphs, other languages, and base64 in the corpus** without being asked. You say you have a seed set, mutators, benign twins, and end-to-end ASR by transform. You say the model can decode more than the filter, so capability removal still matters. That is the whole answer. If they want more, you add split-across-chunks and OCR.

This is the close of the jailbreak module: not a philosophy of layering, a concrete test list.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Many candidates say 'we red team' and cannot name a transform. Naming three makes you sound like you have run a suite. On the job, those three catch a surprising fraction of lazy attacks and keep the suite honest.

Spoken 20 seconds:

We mutate seeds automatically, keep benign look-alikes, and we still fail closed on tools because the model decodes encodings the filter misses.'

## Failure modes

1. **Only listing 'adversarial examples'** with no nouns.

2. **Forgetting the corpus.** They asked about retrieved input, not just the chat box.

3. **Stopping at the list** without residual risk (capability).

When they ask how I test guardrails I name homoglyphs, other languages, and base64 in the corpus, plus mutators and benign twins. I measure end-to-end ASR and I still remove capabilities because the model can decode more than the filter.

Interview close: you write three bullets, one ASR table header, and 'tools fail closed'. The interviewer moves on. That is the point of the item.

## What I would measure

Whether practice answers include those three nouns in under twenty seconds; whether the real suite contains them.

When the interviewer changes the constraints — half the latency budget, a new region, a hostile document, a cheaper model — I keep the same skeleton for **Interview: test obfuscated input** means you volunteer **homoglyphs, other lan and swap the binding constraint. I measure end-to-end ASR and I still remove capabilities because the model can decode more than the filter.

I do not restart from a blank architecture. That is what junior answers do. I show what I would drop first and what I would never drop.

This topic dies when it lives only in a prompt or a wiki page. Prompts regress on the next model bump; wiki pages do not run in CI. I put the control in code and the proof in a test. I also watch for correlated layers that look like depth and fail together.

read-only-vs-consequential-actions.explain:
## What it is

Classify every tool by **consequence**. Read-only / reversible: search, fetch own record, summarise. Write, reversible: create a draft, add a label. Consequential / irreversible: send email, charge a card, delete, deploy, change IAM, post publicly, run a shell.

Match controls to blast radius. Reads can run more freely but still leak and can exfiltrate (a URL with data in the query). Reversible writes need logging and undo. Consequential actions need approval, limits, or both. Prefer **propose then commit**: the agent creates a draft; a deterministic step or a human applies it. Split read and write scopes so a read task cannot invoke a write.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will hand you a tool list and ask you to classify. On the job this table is how you decide where to put a confirm screen without confirming every search.

## How it works + one small example

Table: `search_docs` (read, ACL); `create_draft_email` (write reversible, log); `send_email` (consequential, approve + allow-list); `delete_customer` (consequential, approve + dual control). Idempotency keys on writes.

A 'read-only' `fetch_url` is still dangerous: SSRF and exfil. Treat network as consequential unless the host allow-list is tight and the response cannot leave.

## Failure modes

1. **One policy for all tools.**

2. **Calling fetch read-only** while it can hit metadata IPs.

3. **No undo** on 'reversible' writes that are not actually reversible.

4. **Propose-then-commit that auto-commits** after 50 ms.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I classify tools as read, reversible write, or consequential, and I match controls to blast radius. I prefer propose-then-commit, I split read and write scopes, and I treat fetch as consequential unless the network is fenced.

## A concrete walk-through

You print the tool table in the design doc. Legal circles send and delete. You implement drafts for send and a 24-hour undo for labels. Fetch moves behind a proxy allow-list.

## What I would measure

Share of consequential calls that went through propose-then-commit; auto-approved fraction; fetch calls off the allow-list (should be zero).

## Interview follow-up

If they push on Classify every tool by **consequence**. Read only / reversible: search, fetch ow, I do not invent a second framework. I pick one control, one number, and the residual risk. The points I will not drop: 1) Classify every tool by consequence and reversibility; 2) Match approval and limits to blast radius; 3) Propose then commit for irreversible work; 4) Split read and write tool scopes; 5) Read-only fetch can still exfiltrate or SSRF. If they only have thirty seconds left I repeat the line and stop: I classify tools as read, reversible write, or consequential, and I match controls to blast radius. I prefer propose-then-commit, I split read and write scopes, and I treat fetch as consequential unless the network is fenced.

A common trap is answering a different question — a model-vendor anecdote, a tool name, a blog slogan. I steer back to the boundary or the metric. If they ask what I would cut with a week less, I cut the probabilistic layer first and keep the deterministic one.

## How this fails in a real review

The cheap objection is that this is overkill for a prototype. A prototype can be smaller, but the constraint still belongs in writing so we do not promote the prototype unchanged. Another objection is that the next model will make the problem go away. A better model does not remove a missing ACL, a shared admin token, an unmeasured p95, or a cache key without a tenant. I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What I would do on Monday

I would add one test or one dashboard panel that makes this topic visible, name an owner in the design doc, and put the thirty-second line at the top of the PR. If I cannot name the owner and the metric, I do not understand the work yet. I would rather ship a smaller capability with a measured residual than a demo that fails the first red team or the first traffic spike.

Match approval and limits to blast radius.
Propose then commit for irreversible work.
Split read and write tool scopes.
Read-only fetch can still exfiltrate or SSRF.
Make writes idempotent with request ids.

questions.q: Classify: search_docs, create_draft_email, send_email, delete_customer. State the control for each.
questions.a: search_docs: read, ACL. create_draft_email: reversible write, log and undo. send_email: consequential, approval and recipient allow-list. delete_customer: consequential, approval and a second check or cooling-off.

questions.q: Why can a 'read-only' fetch_url tool still be dangerous?
questions.a: It can reach internal endpoints (SSRF) and it can send private data in the URL. Allow-list hosts, block link-local, and treat it as egress.

questions.q: What does propose-then-commit provide that a prompt warning does not?
questions.a: A durable object the user or a policy engine can inspect and apply. The model never holds the commit tool in the same breath as the untrusted read, if you design it that way.

questions.q: Users approve 99% of send prompts in under a second. What do you change?
questions.a: The screen is not being read. Show arguments, add a delay or typed confirm for high risk, or move more sends to drafts. Approval theatre is not a control.

questions.q: How do you stop a summarise route from calling delete?
questions.a: Do not put delete in that route's schema. Registry separation is stronger than 'please only read'.

validating-tool-use-outside-the-llm.explain:
## What it is

The model **proposes**; your code **disposes**. Validate **selection, arguments, permissions, and outputs** independently of the LLM. Schema (types, enums, ranges) is necessary and not sufficient: a well-typed `delete_file("/etc/passwd")` or `refund(other_customer)` still fails policy. The executor loads the caller's identity, checks authZ, allow-lists verbs and destinations, applies business limits, then runs. After the call, validate the tool result before it re-enters the prompt (size, type, no secrets).

JSON schema validation is hygiene. Policy is the security control.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask where the ownership check lives. 'In the tool description' is wrong. On the job this is the difference between a demo agent and one you can insure.

## How it works + one small example

Before `delete_file(path)`: schema says string; policy says path is under the user's workspace prefix; caller owns the file; path is normalised (no `..`); rate limit; audit log. After: result is a status enum, not a 2 MB dump.

Do not 'fix' invalid args by guessing. Reject. Do not let the model supply `user_id` for authZ. Structured outputs help you parse; they do not authorise.

## Failure modes

1. **Schema only.** Types are not rights.

2. **Repairing args.** You execute a guess.

3. **AuthZ on a model-supplied role.**

4. **Passing raw tool dumps back** as trusted context.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I validate tool selection, arguments, permissions, and outputs in code. Schema is not enough. The executor uses the caller's identity and business limits, rejects bad payloads, and sanitises results before they re-enter the prompt.

## A concrete walk-through

A refund JSON is valid and names another tenant's order. Schema passes; policy fails. You add a unit test with that payload and you never 'helpfully' swap in the current user's latest order.

## What I would measure

Tool-call reject reasons (schema vs authZ vs limit); count of repaired-arg executions (target zero); max tool-result bytes accepted.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on The model **proposes**; your code **disposes**. Validate **selection, arguments, is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) Model proposes; code disposes; 2) Validate selection, args, permissions, and outputs; 3) JSON schema is necessary and not sufficient; 4) Authorise with the caller, not model-supplied ids; 5) Reject invalid args; do not repair them. The spoken close stays the same: I validate tool selection, arguments, permissions, and outputs in code. Schema is not enough. The executor uses the caller's identity and business limits, rejects bad payloads, and sanitises results before they re-enter the prompt.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

## How this fails in a real review

Teams skip this when a demo is due. The skip shows up later as an incident, a surprise bill, or a questionnaire they cannot answer. I write the failure modes into the runbook so the next on-call does not rediscover them. I also refuse a change that cannot be tested, versioned, and rolled back.

## What I would do on Monday

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.

Validate selection, args, permissions, and outputs.
JSON schema is necessary and not sufficient.
Authorise with the caller, not model-supplied ids.
Reject invalid args; do not repair them.
Sanitise tool results before the next turn.

questions.q: List what an executor should verify before running a model-proposed delete_file(path) call.
questions.a: Schema, path normalisation, prefix allow-list, caller ownership, rate limits, and an audit record. Then run. Do not trust a well-typed path.

questions.q: Why isn't JSON schema validation alone enough for security?
questions.a: A payload can be well-typed and still name another customer's id, a disallowed host, or an unbounded amount. Policy and authZ are separate checks.

questions.q: The model sets `acting_as: admin` in the tool JSON. What happens?
questions.a: The executor ignores it. Role comes from the session. Log the attempt. Never promote a field the model wrote into a privilege.

questions.q: What do you validate on the way back from a tool?
questions.a: Size, type, presence of secrets or HTML, and whether the result should be summarised before it re-enters context. Tool output is untrusted text.

questions.q: How do structured outputs change this picture?
questions.a: They make parse failures rare. They do not authorise. Keep the policy engine.

questions.a: The explanation can hide or soften the real recipient, amount, or path. The executor's payload is what will happen. Show that.

questions.q: Users approve 99.5% of prompts within one second. What does that suggest and what do you do?
questions.a: They are not reading. Slow the path, require a typed confirm for high risk, move to drafts, or reduce how often you ask so the remaining asks matter.

questions.q: When is approval the wrong control?
questions.a: For high-volume low-risk reads, or when the user cannot judge the args (raw hashes). Use allow-lists and limits instead of training people to click Yes.

questions.q: What belongs in the audit record of an approval?
questions.a: Actor, timestamp, action type, the arguments shown, the arguments executed, and the session or trace id. Not necessarily the full chat body.

questions.q: How do you implement approval without blocking the HTTP request for ten minutes?
questions.a: Create a pending action object, return it to the UI, resume the pipeline on webhook or poll after click. Do not hold a model context open while someone is at lunch.

step-runtime-cost-limits.explain:
## What it is

Limit **steps, runtime, cost, and tool usage** so a fooled or looping agent cannot run forever. Caps: max model calls, max tool calls, wall-clock timeout, token and dollar budget, per-tool rate limits, max fan-out. On hit: stop, return partial work, alert. Do not retry unbounded.

Limits are security and reliability. An injected page that says 'fetch the next URL' 5,000 times is denial of wallet and a scrape. A research agent without a budget is a blank cheque.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers ask what stops a runaway loop. 'The model will notice' is not an answer. On the job, the first weekend an agent is live is when you learn whether the cap exists.

## How it works + one small example

Example research agent: 20 model calls, 40 tool calls, 3 minutes, $0.50, 5 fetches per host, no recursive fetch of the same URL. The harness enforces this; the prompt can mention it but cannot raise it.

When a run hits a cap, persist the trace, show the user a 'stopped: budget' state, and do not silently continue in a background worker with a higher cap unless that is a billed, approved job.

## Failure modes

1. **Limits only in the prompt.**

2. **Catching errors by retrying** into the same loop.

3. **A global budget** one batch job can exhaust for everyone.

4. **No user-visible stop reason.** They retry and double spend.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I cap agent steps, runtime, cost, and tool fan-out in the harness. When a limit hits I stop, show why, and alert. Those caps are security controls against loops and denial of wallet, not just cost hygiene.

## A concrete walk-through

Staging: a payload loops browse. Cost hits $0.50 and dies at call 20. You add the same cap to prod and a dashboard panel for 'stopped: budget' rate.

## What I would measure

Runs stopped by each cap; dollars per successful task; p99 tool-call count; shared-wallet starvation events.

## Interview follow-up

When the interviewer changes the constraints — half the latency budget, a new region, a hostile document, a cheaper model — I keep the same skeleton for Limit **steps, runtime, cost, and tool usage** so a fooled or looping agent cann and swap the binding constraint. The skeleton is: 1) Cap steps, wall time, tokens, dollars, and per-tool rates; 2) Enforce in the harness, not in the prompt; 3) On hit: stop, persist, tell the user, alert; 4) Limits stop injected loops and wallet abuse; 5) Per-feature budgets beat one global pool. The sentence I can say under pressure is: I cap agent steps, runtime, cost, and tool fan-out in the harness. When a limit hits I stop, show why, and alert. Those caps are security controls against loops and denial of wallet, not just cost hygiene.

I do not restart from a blank architecture. That is what junior answers do. I show what I would drop first and what I would never drop.

## How this fails in a real review

This topic dies when it lives only in a prompt or a wiki page. Prompts regress on the next model bump; wiki pages do not run in CI. I put the control in code and the proof in a test. I also watch for correlated layers that look like depth and fail together.

## What I would do on Monday

I would pair with the owner of the executor, the retriever, or the gateway — whichever box this topic touches — and add the smallest check that would have caught last quarter's near-miss. Then I would re-run the relevant suite or eval and write the delta in the release notes.

Enforce in the harness, not in the prompt.

Retries must share the same remaining budget.

questions.q: Which limits would you put on an autonomous research agent?
questions.a: Max model and tool calls, wall-clock, dollar budget, per-host fetch cap, and a duplicate-URL block. Enforce in the harness and surface a stopped-for-budget state.

questions.q: An injected page makes the agent fetch 5,000 URLs. Which controls would have helped?
questions.a: A fetch count cap, per-host rate limit, duplicate URL block, dollar budget, and no recursive fetch tool. Prompt text would not have helped.

questions.q: A run hits its max-step limit with the task unfinished. The best behaviour is?
questions.a: Stop, return partial results and the reason, keep the trace, do not silently raise the cap. The user can start a billed continuation.

questions.q: Why must retries share the remaining budget?
questions.a: Otherwise a failing provider turns one request into N full runs and the cap is fiction.

questions.q: How do you stop one batch job from starving interactive chat?
questions.a: Separate quotas and queues per class of traffic. Caps are per feature, not one shared wallet.

## What it is

Treat generated **SQL, shell, URLs, and code** as untrusted programs. Run them in a **sandbox**: no production credentials, no tenant crossover, tight CPU/memory/time, no raw host network (or an allow-listed proxy), a fresh filesystem, and an identity that is not your app's. Multi-tenant analysis tools need a new jail per session.

The model is a source of code, not an operator. If you cannot say what the sandbox blocks, you do not have one — you have `eval` on the app server.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will offer a 'data analysis copilot' and wait for you to mention isolation. On the job, this is how you avoid a generated `os.system` reading `os.environ`.

## How it works + one small example

Example. Users upload CSVs; the model writes pandas. You run in a container or Wasm jail: only that CSV mounted, no env secrets, 30 s, 512 MB, no egress except a result blob store. SQL goes to a read-only role on a clone, statement allow-list, row cap.

Network in the sandbox is the difference between 'plot this' and 'curl the metadata service'. Default deny.

## Failure modes

1. **Running on the API host** with the app's env.

2. **One long-lived notebook kernel** for all tenants.

3. **Allowing pip install from the internet** in the jail.

4. **Passing the same DB writer role** the app uses.

Generated code, SQL, commands, and URLs are untrusted. I run them in a sandbox with no production secrets, no cross-tenant disk, tight limits, and default-deny network. If it is `eval` on the app host, it is not shipped.

## A concrete walk-through

A demo ran generated Python in Flask. You rip it out, add a gVisor or Wasm worker, and write a test that `os.environ` is empty and that a curl to the metadata IP fails.

## What I would measure

questions.a: Per-session jail, only that tenant's file mounted, no env secrets, CPU/memory/time caps, no egress or an allow-listed result store, destroy after the run. Never a shared kernel.

## What it is

**Recipients, URLs, and verbs are decided by the server**, not by the model's prose and not by a 'please only call these' sentence. The executor holds an allow-list: hosts, HTTP methods, email domains, SQL verbs, IAM actions. Unknown destinations fail. Allow-lists are code, reviewed, and tested. They are the difference between 'we have tools' and 'we have a programmable proxy'.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the interview sentence that shows you have written an executor. On the job it is the PR security actually approves.

questions.a: The destination and verb are fixed. The model cannot turn a knowledge read into a general HTTP client.

human-approval-as-a-product-feature.explain:
## What it is

**Show the draft action and wait; do not auto-send.** This is the product wording of approval: a first-class pending state, a UI that is readable on a phone, a timeout that expires to 'not sent' rather than 'sent', and analytics on skip-through. It is not a toast that disappears.

Engineering owns the pending object and the exact args. Design owns the screen. Support owns what happens when someone is offline. If any of those are missing, you have a library flag, not a feature.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Security reviews fail when approval is a boolean in a framework. Interviewers ask how a user on mobile sees a refund. If you cannot describe the screen, you have not designed the control.

## How it works + one small example

PendingAction: id, verb, args, created_at, expires_at, state. UI: readable fields, diffs for edits, danger colour for irreversible. Expire → cancelled. Notify the owner. Resume the pipeline only on explicit confirm.

Do not hide this behind 'the agent will just send if you do not reply' unless that is a separately consented digest with a fixed template.

## Failure modes

1. **Auto-send on timeout.**

2. **Desktop-only modal** for an on-call mobile audience.

3. **No pending object** — approval is a chat message the model can spoof.

4. **Feature flag default on** without UX.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Approval is a product feature: a pending draft, a readable screen, wait, expire to not-sent, and metrics on skip-through. I do not auto-send, and I do not implement this as a disappearing toast.

## A concrete walk-through

You replace 'OK to send?' in the chat with a PendingSend card in the app. Silence cancels. Support uses the same card. The model can no longer print a fake 'approved' token.

## What I would measure

Expire-to-cancel count; approve latency distribution; spoofed-approval attempts in logs; mobile completion rate.

## What it is

Retrieved documents are **untrusted data**, not trusted instructions, even when they come from 'your' index. The index is a store of strings. Integrity of operations is not integrity of content. Public pages, vendor PDFs, and employee wiki edits all become commands if you paste them raw next to the system prompt.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

4. **No citation**, so you cannot see which chunk steered the answer.

## What it is

**Cross-tenant leakage** is tenant A's data appearing in tenant B's prompt, cache, log, or answer. It hides in more places than the vector query: embeddings stored without a tenant key, a semantic cache keyed only on the question, a shared memory store, rerank calls that send mixed batches to a vendor, eval sets, traces, screenshots, and support exports.

Defence is **isolation you cannot forget**: separate indexes or a mandatory tenant filter, cache keys that include tenant, no shared 'global' memory, and tests that try to retrieve the other tenant's canary. A similarity search that is only approximately isolated is not isolated.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is an enterprise-deal breaker. Interviewers will mention a semantic cache as the leak. On the job, one leaked chunk can be a contract-ending event.

## How it works + one small example

Design: tenant on every row; queries always `AND tenant_id =`; cache key `hash(tenant, route, question)`; memory partitioned; vendor rerank sends only already-filtered ids; evals use synthetic or consented data per tenant.

Test: insert canary C_A only in A; user B asks the question that would retrieve C_A; assert C_A never appears in chunks, prompt, answer, or cache. Repeat after a cache fill from A.

## Failure modes

1. **Cache key = embedding(question)** only.

2. **One index, filter optional** in a helper you forgot to call.

3. **Support admin UI** that searches globally and then pastes into a tenant chat.

4. **Fine-tunes** on mixed-tenant logs.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Cross-tenant leakage hides in queries, caches, memories, rerank batches, logs, and evals. I isolate with mandatory tenant filters or separate indexes, I key caches on tenant, and I test with canaries I cannot forget.

## A concrete walk-through

You find the cache key is only the embedding. You add tenant and route, flush, and the canary test goes green. You add the same test for the admin export job.

Canary failures (page); cache keys missing tenant; global search uses outside admin audit.

The sentence I can say under pressure is: Cross-tenant leakage hides in queries, caches, memories, rerank batches, logs, and evals. preserving-provenance.explain:
## What it is

**Provenance** is the record of *where a retrieved string came from*: document id, URI, version, offset, hash, timestamp, tenant, and the query that fetched it. You store it with the chunk, pass ids into the prompt, show citations, and keep the mapping in the trace even if you do not show every field to the user.

Without provenance you cannot takedown, cannot audit a poisoning, cannot honour deletion, and cannot tell a user which policy you quoted. Summaries written to memory without a source are how poisoned text becomes 'the system's belief'.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Incident response for RAG is impossible if you cannot name the page. Interviewers ask why citations are a security control, not only UX. On the job, provenance is how legal and security finish the week.

## How it works + one small example

Each chunk: `{doc_id, version, hash, span, uri, tenant}`. The answer emits citation ids. The trace stores the exact chunk hashes in the prompt. A memory write stores the same ids. If you summarise a web page, the memory row keeps the URL and retrieval time.

When a user says 'the bot invented a policy', you open the trace and see whether a real span supported it. When security says 'remove this PDF', you find every chunk hash and every memory that cited it.

## Failure modes

1. **Citations as decoration** not tied to stored spans.

2. **Memory summaries with no source.**

3. **Re-embedding that drops version.**

4. **User-facing citations that point to a document the user cannot open** (ACL leak by title).

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I preserve provenance — id, version, hash, span, tenant — on every chunk, citation, trace, and memory write. Without it I cannot takedown, delete, or defend an answer, and a poisoned summary becomes untraceable belief.

## A concrete walk-through

A bad answer cites 'policy v3'. You pull the trace, hash-match the span, and find a draft PDF that should not have been indexed. Takedown is a query on `doc_id`, not a guess.

## What I would measure

Share of answers with resolvable citations; memories missing a source; time to list all uses of a doc_id.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on **Provenance** is the record of *where a retrieved string came from*: document i is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) Provenance is id, version, hash, span, uri, tenant; 2) Citations, traces, and memories all carry it; 3) You cannot takedown or erase what you cannot find; 4) A sourceless memory is a provenance bug; 5) Do not cite a title the user is not allowed to see. The spoken close stays the same: I preserve provenance — id, version, hash, span, tenant — on every chunk, citation, trace, and memory write. Without it I cannot takedown, delete, or defend an answer, and a poisoned summary becomes untraceable belief.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

## How this fails in a real review

Teams skip this when a demo is due. The skip shows up later as an incident, a surprise bill, or a questionnaire they cannot answer. I write the failure modes into the runbook so the next on-call does not rediscover them. I also refuse a change that cannot be tested, versioned, and rolled back.

## What I would do on Monday

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.

Hashes let you prove which bytes were in the prompt.

questions.a: You need to find every use of a poisoned or revoked document: chunks, prompts, answers, caches, and memories. Without ids and hashes you cannot takedown or explain what the model saw.

questions.a: Showing a forbidden document's title or URL tells the user it exists. Only cite what the ACL already allowed into the prompt.

questions.a: doc_id, version, content hash, tenant, uri, and span. That is enough to find and delete descendants.

per-document-acls-at-retrieve-time.explain:
## What it is

**Filter before ANN, not after the model saw the text.** This is the sharp form of document permissions. Approximate nearest neighbour over the whole corpus and then drop forbidden hits still **loaded those vectors, often those texts, and sometimes those texts into a reranker or a prompt draft**. That is late.

Do the permission predicate in the same query, or ANN inside a precomputed allowed set. If your vendor cannot, change vendor or maintain per-principal indexes. 'We usually post-filter' is a leak with a high hit rate on popular docs.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers listen for 'before ANN'. It is the phrase that shows you have felt this bug. On the job it is the PR that closes a red finding.

## How it works + one small example

Bad: `top_20 = ann(query); return [d for d in top_20 if allowed(user, d)][:5]`. The model or reranker may already have 20, including secrets, and you might return fewer than 5 without noticing why.

Good: `ann(query, filter=acl(user))` or `ann(query, index=user_or_tenant_index)`. Tests: a secret doc is the nearest neighbour globally; the allowed user never sees it in traces.

## Failure modes

1. **Rerank vendor** receiving unfiltered text.

2. **Debug logs** of the unfiltered top-20.

3. **Assuming ANN+filter is equivalent** because 'we do not send leftovers to the model' — leftovers were still processed.

4. **Empty results** when all top-k were forbidden, silently.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Per-document ACLs apply at retrieve time, before ANN or inside a filtered search, not after the model or a reranker saw the text. Post-filter is a leak. I test with a globally nearest secret that must never appear in traces.

## A concrete walk-through

Security reproduces a secret doc as neighbour #1. Your old code post-filtered it but logged the title. You switch to filtered ANN and delete title logs. The canary test is now in CI.

## What I would measure

Traces containing forbidden ids; rerank batches with mixed ACLs; queries using the unfiltered helper.

## Interview follow-up

poisoned-corpus-as-a-first-class-threat.explain:
## What it is

An **insider or a public page can rewrite behaviour**. Treat a poisoned corpus as a planned threat, not a trivia item. Threat-model who can write what you retrieve: employees, vendors, crawlers, end users (tickets), attackers on the public web. Give each writer a trust tier. High-impact queries (HR, finance, medical, admin) retrieve only from high tiers or from reviewed snapshots.

This item is the mindset: the corpus is an input surface with authors, not a library that is 'just there'.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Teams underinvest here because it feels like content ops. Interviewers use it to see if you connect RAG to insider threat. On the job it changes who can publish to the index.

## How it works + one small example

Tiers: `reviewed_policy`, `internal_wiki`, `tickets`, `web`. HR bot retrieves only `reviewed_policy`. Support copilot can use wiki plus tickets but wraps tickets as untrusted and cannot change policy answers from a ticket.

Publishing to `reviewed_policy` is a two-person review and a signed snapshot. Web crawl never lands in that tier. An insider who can edit the wiki cannot edit the snapshot without the second person.

## Failure modes

1. **One corpus for every route.**

2. **Crawling the web into HR.**

3. **No author tier** so a ticket can override a policy.

4. **Calling this 'just quality'** and skipping security review.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A poisoned corpus is a first-class threat: an insider or a public page can rewrite behaviour. I tier writers, I restrict high-impact routes to reviewed snapshots, and I never let tickets or the web override policy silently.

## A concrete walk-through

You split indexes by tier. The HR route's config lists one snapshot id. A wiki vandalism incident no longer changes parental-leave answers. Support still sees the wiki, wrapped.

## What I would measure

Routes whose allowed tiers are documented; promotions to reviewed without two approvers; incidents where a low tier overrode a high tier.

## Interview follow-up

If they push on An **insider or a public page can rewrite behaviour**. Treat a poisoned corpus a, I do not invent a second framework. I pick one control, one number, and the residual risk. The points I will not drop: 1) Who can write what you retrieve is a threat-model question; 2) Tier sources; high-impact routes use reviewed snapshots; 3) Insiders and public pages are both authors; 4) Tickets must not silently override policy; 5) This is security, not only content quality. If they only have thirty seconds left I repeat the line and stop: A poisoned corpus is a first-class threat: an insider or a public page can rewrite behaviour. I tier writers, I restrict high-impact routes to reviewed snapshots, and I never let tickets or the web override policy silently.

A common trap is answering a different question — a model-vendor anecdote, a tool name, a blog slogan. I steer back to the boundary or the metric. If they ask what I would cut with a week less, I cut the probabilistic layer first and keep the deterministic one.

## How this fails in a real review

The cheap objection is that this is overkill for a prototype. A prototype can be smaller, but the constraint still belongs in writing so we do not promote the prototype unchanged. Another objection is that the next model will make the problem go away. A better model does not remove a missing ACL, a shared admin token, an unmeasured p95, or a cache key without a tenant. I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What I would do on Monday

I would add one test or one dashboard panel that makes this topic visible, name an owner in the design doc, and put the thirty-second line at the top of the PR. If I cannot name the owner and the metric, I do not understand the work yet. I would rather ship a smaller capability with a measured residual than a demo that fails the first red team or the first traffic spike.

Tier sources; high-impact routes use reviewed snapshots.
Insiders and public pages are both authors.
Tickets must not silently override policy.
This is security, not only content quality.
Two-person review for the highest tier.

questions.a: It changes behaviour for many users, can inject commands, and can be planted by an insider or a public page. That is integrity and injection, not a typo.

questions.a: Reviewed policy snapshots for HR; wiki for support with wrappers; tickets as untrusted; web never in HR. Routes declare allowed tiers.

questions.a: Anyone who can publish or compromise a page you fetch. That set is unbounded; keep web out of high-impact routes.

questions.a: Two-person review, signed snapshot, and an audit of who promoted the doc. Edit on a wiki is not enough.

## What it is

**Detect, redact, mask, or drop** sensitive information before it goes to a model when the model does not need it. Minimization is the first choice: do not send the field. Redaction replaces with a typed placeholder (`[EMAIL_1]`) so the task can continue. Masking hides part of a value. **Pseudonymisation** maps an identity to a stable token you can reverse in a secure store after the model returns.

A **redact-then-restore** pipeline: replace PII with placeholders, call the model, then restore placeholders in the user-visible output if policy allows — never restore into logs. The model should see `please refund [ORDER_1]` not the raw PAN.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you use an external LLM on support tickets without mailing the provider your customers. Interviewers want the pipeline, not 'we redact'. On the job, restore-into-logs is the bug.

## How it works + one small example

Example. Ticket in → detect emails, phones, order ids → replace with numbered tokens → send to the model → model writes a reply using tokens → restore only in the agent UI → logs keep tokens. Order id might stay if the model must look it up; then the lookup is a tool with authZ, and the id never needed to be in the prose.

Do not minimize so hard the task dies (dropping the error code). Measure task success on a redacted eval set.

1. **Restore into traces.**

2. **Unstable tokens** so the model cannot refer to the same person twice.

3. **Redacting after the provider call.**

4. **One global redaction policy** that breaks medical or legal routes that need more context under a stricter hosting model.

## A concrete walk-through

You ship redact-then-restore for email. Quality holds on the eval set. A debug flag had been restoring into JSON logs; you delete that path and rotate access to old files.

PII fields reaching the provider; task success on redacted versus raw (raw only in a secure harness); traces containing restored values.

retention-deletion-residency.explain:
## What it is

Know **how long** each store keeps data, **how you delete** it, **where** it lives, **who** can access it, and **what the model provider** does (training, retention, subprocessors, regions). Retention is a legal setting, not a disk-cleanup habit. Deletion is a pipeline: primary DB, indexes, caches, memories, traces, evals, backups per policy. Residency is pinning processing and storage to a region when a customer or law requires it.

A deletion request that only hits Mongo and forgets the vector store is a failed request. A 'EU-only' story that still sends prompts to a US-only endpoint is a failed story.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

DPDP, GDPR, and enterprise DPAs all land here. Interviewers ask for the store list. On the job this is the security questionnaire.

## How it works + one small example

Table per store: purpose, TTL, region, delete API, backup story, access role. Provider column: zero-retention option, training off, region, DPA.

Example. Customer demands EU-only. You review: app region, vector region, provider region, log vendor region, and whether any fallback model is US. You refuse a fallback that breaks residency rather than silently succeeding.

## Failure modes

1. **TTL on the ticket, forever on the index.**

2. **Backups that cannot delete** and no exception process.

3. **Provider default training-on** because someone used the consumer API.

4. **Residency as a marketing label** without pinning the client.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Retention, deletion, and residency are a table: every store, a TTL, a delete path, a region, and a provider row. I honour erasure across indexes and evals, and I will fail a request rather than silently process in the wrong region.

## A concrete walk-through

A DPA questionnaire arrives. You attach the store table. One row is empty (eval bucket). You add TTL and a delete job before you sign.

## What I would measure

Stores with a tested delete; fallbacks that broke residency in staging; time to complete an erasure drill.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on Know **how long** each store keeps data, **how you delete** it, **where** it liv is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) Every store has purpose, TTL, region, and a delete path; 2) Erasure includes vectors, caches, memories, evals, and traces; 3) Provider training and retention are explicit settings; 4) Residency is pinned in the client, including fallbacks; 5) Backups need a documented story. The spoken close stays the same: Retention, deletion, and residency are a table: every store, a TTL, a delete path, a region, and a provider row. protecting-secrets-from-the-model.explain:
## What it is

**Secrets never need to be in the prompt.** API keys, session tokens, passwords, private keys, and connection strings live in the **executor** or a secret manager. The model sees a tool name and arguments; the server injects the credential at call time. If the model must call a payment API, it proposes `charge(order_id)`; your code loads the key.

Also prevent secrets from *entering* context: users paste curl with bearer tokens; retrieved docs contain keys; tool errors echo credentials. Detect and drop. Once a secret is in context it can be printed, cached, logged, or stuffed into a URL.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is a hard interview line. 'The model needs the key to call the API' is a fail. On the job, pasted tokens in chat are a weekly event.

## How it works + one small example

Pattern: tool adapter holds the secret; model never lists env; sandbox env is stripped. User paste: a detector strips `Authorization:` and rotates if it looks live. Retrieved files: secret scan before index. Tool errors: sanitise.

If a user pastes a token, you treat it as a leak: redact, warn, and tell them to rotate. Do not store it in history.

## Failure modes

1. **Keys in the system prompt** 'for function calling'.

2. **Passing `process.env` into the sandbox.**

3. **Logging tool args** that accidentally included a user-pasted secret.

4. **Asking the model to 'remember my key'.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The model never needs the key. I inject secrets in the executor, I strip them from user paste and retrieval, and I treat anything that reached context as a leak to rotate.

## A concrete walk-through

You remove `OPENAI_API_KEY` from the tool-worker env (it only needs the downstream billing key in a sidecar). A paste detector lands on the chat API. One week later it catches a GitHub token and opens a rotate ticket.

## What I would measure

Secret-scanner hits in prompts; keys present in model-visible env; time-to-rotate after a paste detect.

## Interview follow-up

If they push on **Secrets never need to be in the prompt.** API keys, session tokens, passwords,, I do not invent a second framework. I pick one control, one number, and the residual risk. The points I will not drop: 1) Secrets live in the executor or a secret manager; 2) The model proposes actions, not credentials; 3) Scan user paste, retrieval, and tool errors; 4) A secret in context is a leak: redact and rotate; 5) Sandbox environments are stripped. If they only have thirty seconds left I repeat the line and stop: The model never needs the key. I inject secrets in the executor, I strip them from user paste and retrieval, and I treat anything that reached context as a leak to rotate.

A common trap is answering a different question — a model-vendor anecdote, a tool name, a blog slogan. I steer back to the boundary or the metric. If they ask what I would cut with a week less, I cut the probabilistic layer first and keep the deterministic one.

## How this fails in a real review

The cheap objection is that this is overkill for a prototype. A prototype can be smaller, but the constraint still belongs in writing so we do not promote the prototype unchanged. Another objection is that the next model will make the problem go away. A better model does not remove a missing ACL, a shared admin token, an unmeasured p95, or a cache key without a tenant. I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What I would do on Monday

I would add one test or one dashboard panel that makes this topic visible, name an owner in the design doc, and put the thirty-second line at the top of the PR. If I cannot name the owner and the metric, I do not understand the work yet. I would rather ship a smaller capability with a measured residual than a demo that fails the first red team or the first traffic spike.

The model proposes actions, not credentials.
Scan user paste, retrieval, and tool errors.
A secret in context is a leak: redact and rotate.
Sandbox environments are stripped.
Do not log args that may contain pasted tokens.

questions.q: How should an agent call an API that needs a key without exposing the key to the model?
questions.a: The model emits a typed tool call. The executor loads the key from a secret manager and calls the API. The key never appears in messages.

questions.q: A user pastes a curl command with a bearer token into the chat. What happens and what should the system do?
questions.a: The token is now in context, history, and maybe logs. Detect, redact, warn, drop from history, and tell them to rotate. Do not store or send it to the provider if you can stop it first.

questions.q: Where should a payment-API key live?
questions.a: In the executor's secret store, injected at call time. Not in the prompt, the tool description, or the browser.

questions.q: Why scan retrieved files for secrets?
questions.a: Engineers commit keys; the index will happily retrieve them into other users' prompts.

questions.q: What do you do if a secret reached a provider log?
questions.a: Rotate, request deletion per the DPA, and fix the detector. Treat it as an incident, not as 'the model saw it once'.

## What it is

An **adversarial test suite** is a versioned set of attacks you run against the **whole product**, not the model card: prompt injection (direct and indirect), jailbreaks, malicious documents, tool misuse, data extraction, and unsafe agent actions. Each case has a **goal**, a **payload**, an **oracle** (did the secret leak, did the tool fire, did the policy drop), and an expected **control**.

The suite is living: new jailbreaks become cases. It includes obfuscations and benign twins. You run it in CI and on a cadence against staging with production-like tools and a fake corpus. Model-only evals miss the renderer, the executor, and the retriever.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

## How it works + one small example

1. **Testing the model API** without tools or retrieval.

2. **LLM-as-oracle only.**

3. **A static list** you never mutate.

4. **No benign twins**, so you 'fix' attacks by blocking half of real traffic.

I build a versioned adversarial suite against the whole pipeline — injection, jailbreaks, poisoned docs, tool misuse, extraction — with hard oracles, mutators, and benign twins. New attacks become cases. Model-only tests are not enough.

## A concrete walk-through

You add ten seeds, three mutators, and canary oracles to CI. A prompt tweak fails the refund case. That is the suite working. You do not revert to 'it looked fine in chat'.

questions.a: Seed goals, payloads (including indirect and obfuscated), hard oracles, expected controls, mutators, benign twins, and a runner that uses the real harness.

questions.q: Why test the whole pipeline rather than the model alone?
questions.a: Retrieval, rendering, and the executor are where exfil and actions happen. A model refusal does not mean the app was safe, and a model compliance does not mean the tool ran.

attacking-rag-through-the-corpus.explain:
## What it is

Red-team RAG by **injecting malicious content into retrievable documents**, not only by typing in the chat box. Plant visible and hidden text, near-duplicates that rank, instruction-in-doc payloads, and canary-marked bait. Use a shared-drive or wiki-shaped fixture that matches production writers.

Success is: the chunk is retrieved for a target query, and then a goal lands (wrong policy, exfil, tool call). Measure both retrieval of the bait and downstream harm. Hidden-text docs belong here because reviewers will not see them in a screenshot.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want this exercise by name. On the job it is how you find that your reader keeps HTML comments.

## How it works + one small example

Outline: create a staging corpus; plant a bait page with a unique command and a unique canary; ask the questions you care about (refund, HR, admin); record whether the bait ranked, whether it entered the prompt, and whether a tool fired. Repeat with comments, `display:none`, and metadata.

A shared-drive exercise adds the insider: a low-privilege editor. If they can change the HR bot, you have a tiering bug.

## Failure modes

1. **Only chat-box injection** on a RAG product.

2. **Planting bait that never ranks**, then declaring victory.

3. **No hidden-text fixtures.**

4. **Forgetting caches** so a delete looks like a pass.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I attack RAG through the corpus: plant visible and hidden bait, check that it ranks, and see whether a goal lands. A chat-box-only red team misses the enterprise path.

## A concrete walk-through

You plant three FAQ variants. Two rank. One causes a send. You fix the reader and the send gate, and you keep the pages as fixtures.

## What I would measure

Bait retrieval rate; goal ASR given retrieval; hidden-text inclusion rate; takedown completeness.

## Interview follow-up

When the interviewer changes the constraints — half the latency budget, a new region, a hostile document, a cheaper model — I keep the same skeleton for Red team RAG by **injecting malicious content into retrievable documents**, not  and swap the binding constraint. The skeleton is: 1) Plant documents; do not only type in chat; 2) Measure rank, prompt inclusion, and downstream harm; 3) Include hidden text and near-duplicates; 4) A low-privilege editor is a realistic actor; 5) Caches can hide a failed takedown. The sentence I can say under pressure is: I attack RAG through the corpus: plant visible and hidden bait, check that it ranks, and see whether a goal lands. A chat-box-only red team misses the enterprise path.

I do not restart from a blank architecture. That is what junior answers do. I show what I would drop first and what I would never drop.

## How this fails in a real review

This topic dies when it lives only in a prompt or a wiki page. Prompts regress on the next model bump; wiki pages do not run in CI. I put the control in code and the proof in a test. I also watch for correlated layers that look like depth and fail together.

## What I would do on Monday

I would pair with the owner of the executor, the retriever, or the gateway — whichever box this topic touches — and add the smallest check that would have caught last quarter's near-miss. Then I would re-run the relevant suite or eval and write the delta in the release notes.

Canary-marked bait makes oracles easy.

questions.a: They look clean to humans and still reach extractors and models. The suite must prove the reader drops them or that tools still refuse.
