questions.a: If the canary appears in a prompt or answer you have retrieval of bait or a leak. If it appears for the wrong tenant you have isolation failure.

questions.q: The bait never ranks. Have you tested injection?
questions.a: Not really. Tune the bait to rank or force-include it once to test the assembler, but also fix ranking assumptions — attackers will SEO the embedding.

questions.q: What two numbers do you report after a corpus attack?
questions.a: Retrieval rate of bait on the target query set, and downstream goal-success rate given retrieval.

attacking-agents-through-their-tools.explain:
## What it is

Red-team agents by trying to make them **exceed permissions, misuse tools, reveal secrets, or loop**. Payloads target the tool loop: 'call refund again', 'fetch the metadata IP', 'cat the env', 'ignore the confirm'. A **malicious MCP server** can attack without a document: hostile tool descriptions, oversized results, or lookalike tool names.

Invariants are better than vibes: `refund.amount <= policy`; `url host in allow-list`; `secrets never in messages`; `steps <= N`. A finding is an invariant violation, not 'the model was naughty'.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the agent-specific suite. Interviewers ask for invariants. On the job, MCP supply chain is the new extra case.

## How it works + one small example

Cases: over-permission (shared admin), argument injection (path traversal), secret reveal (print env), loop (recursive fetch), confused deputy (act on planted text), hostile MCP (tool description says 'send keys here').

Run with the real executor. If the invariant holds when the model is fully compliant with the payload, you pass. If you only pass because the model refused, you have a brittle pass.

## Failure modes

1. **Oracles that are 'the model said no'.**

2. **No MCP or plugin case.**

3. **Not trying loops** because they are 'reliability'.

4. **Testing tools in isolation** without untrusted context.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I attack agents through their tools: permissions, args, secrets, loops, and hostile plugins. I write invariants the executor must hold even if the model complies with the attacker.

## A concrete walk-through

You add an invariant test: `send` destination not in allow-list must throw, with the model output forced to request it. The test does not talk to a live model. That is the point.

## What I would measure

Invariants as automated tests; MCP servers reviewed; runs that passed only via model refusal.

## Interview follow-up

If they push on Red team agents by trying to make them **exceed permissions, misuse tools, revea, I do not invent a second framework. I pick one control, one number, and the residual risk. The points I will not drop: 1) Goals: exceed permission, misuse tools, leak secrets, loop; 2) Invariants beat 'the model refused'; 3) Include hostile MCP or plugin descriptions; 4) Test with untrusted context in the same session; 5) A pass that depends on model refusal is brittle. If they only have thirty seconds left I repeat the line and stop: I attack agents through their tools: permissions, args, secrets, loops, and hostile plugins. I write invariants the executor must hold even if the model complies with the attacker.

A common trap is answering a different question — a model-vendor anecdote, a tool name, a blog slogan. I steer back to the boundary or the metric. If they ask what I would cut with a week less, I cut the probabilistic layer first and keep the deterministic one.

## How this fails in a real review

The cheap objection is that this is overkill for a prototype. A prototype can be smaller, but the constraint still belongs in writing so we do not promote the prototype unchanged. Another objection is that the next model will make the problem go away. A better model does not remove a missing ACL, a shared admin token, an unmeasured p95, or a cache key without a tenant. I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What I would do on Monday

I would add one test or one dashboard panel that makes this topic visible, name an owner in the design doc, and put the thirty-second line at the top of the PR. If I cannot name the owner and the metric, I do not understand the work yet. I would rather ship a smaller capability with a measured residual than a demo that fails the first red team or the first traffic spike.
keyPoints: Goals: exceed permission, misuse tools, leak secrets, loop.
Invariants beat 'the model refused'.
Include hostile MCP or plugin descriptions.
Test with untrusted context in the same session.
A pass that depends on model refusal is brittle.
Loops are security and wallet cases.

questions.q: What invariants would you assert when red-teaming an agent's tool use?
questions.a: AuthZ (caller owns the object), allow-listed destinations, amount and rate limits, no secrets in messages, and step or cost caps. Fail if any break even when the model tries.

questions.q: How could a malicious MCP server attack an agent without a prompt-injecting document?
questions.a: Hostile tool descriptions, lookalike names, huge results that inject on the way back, or a tool that exfiltrates arguments. Treat servers as untrusted code and data.

questions.q: In an agent red team, which finding is expressed as an invariant violation?
questions.a: Example: refund exceeded the policy max, or a URL left the allow-list. That is a testable finding, not a narrative.

questions.q: Why is 'the model refused to call delete' a weak pass?
questions.a: The next model or a better payload will comply. The executor should have rejected delete regardless.

questions.q: How do you test a loop without melting staging?
questions.a: Low caps in the test harness, a payload that would recurse, and an oracle that the cap fired and no extra side effects occurred.

vulnerabilities-become-regression-tests.explain:
## What it is

Every discovered hole becomes a **permanent regression test** in the repo: the payload, the fixture, the oracle, and the control you shipped. Prompt-only fixes without a test come back on the next model upgrade. Stochastic attacks run **multiple times**; a 1/10 pass is not green.

The test should fail if someone reverts the executor check even when the current model 'would not do that'. Prefer deterministic harness tests plus a smaller live-model sample.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you stop whack-a-mole. Interviewers ask what you add to the repo after a prompt-leak. On the job, it is the definition of done for a security ticket.

## How it works + one small example

After a leak: add a canary oracle test; add the exact payload and two mutators; pin the control (renderer blocks images). CI runs the deterministic half on every PR. Nightly runs the live-model half n=10.

If you fixed by editing the system prompt, the test still must fail when that sentence is removed *and* when it is present but the renderer is gone — so you learn which control actually holds.

## Failure modes

1. **Closing the ticket with a prompt PR and no test.**

2. **n=1** on a stochastic attack.

3. **A test so tied to wording** it fails on harmless refactors.

4. **Leaving the fixture only in a chat transcript.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Each vulnerability becomes a regression test: payload, oracle, and the control we shipped. I run stochastic cases more than once, and I do not close a prompt-only fix without a test that would catch the next model upgrade.

## A concrete walk-through

Incident IR-214 becomes `tests/redteam/ir214_image_exfil.py`. The next model bump fails it; you keep the renderer fix and update the prompt later.

## What I would measure

Incidents without a linked test; suite runs on model bumps; flake rate of stochastic cases.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on Every discovered hole becomes a **permanent regression test** in the repo: the p is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) Done means a test in the repo, not a prompt edit; 2) Include payload, fixture, oracle, and control; 3) Run stochastic attacks multiple times; 4) Prefer executor tests that do not need a live model; 5) The next upgrade will regress prompt-only fixes. The spoken close stays the same: Each vulnerability becomes a regression test: payload, oracle, and the control we shipped. I run stochastic cases more than once, and I do not close a prompt-only fix without a test that would catch the next model upgrade.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

## How this fails in a real review

Teams skip this when a demo is due. The skip shows up later as an incident, a surprise bill, or a questionnaire they cannot answer. I write the failure modes into the runbook so the next on-call does not rediscover them. I also refuse a change that cannot be tested, versioned, and rolled back.

## What I would do on Monday

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.
keyPoints: Done means a test in the repo, not a prompt edit.
Include payload, fixture, oracle, and control.
Run stochastic attacks multiple times.
Prefer executor tests that do not need a live model.
The next upgrade will regress prompt-only fixes.
Fixtures live in git, not in a Slack thread.

questions.q: After fixing a prompt-leak bug by editing the system prompt, what should you add to the repo?
questions.a: A canary oracle, the payload plus mutators, and a test of the durable control (renderer or tool denial). Do not rely on the new sentence alone.

questions.q: Why run stochastic attack tests multiple times?
questions.a: Sampling means a single refusal is luck. Report k/n and require a threshold, or prefer a deterministic executor oracle.

questions.q: A vulnerability was fixed by prompt wording. What additional step prevents recurrence after a model upgrade?
questions.a: A regression test on the pipeline plus a control that is not the prompt. Re-run the suite on every model bump.

questions.q: Why should an executor test not need a live model?
questions.a: You can force the bad tool call and assert deny. That still passes when the model changes.

questions.q: Where should the fixture live?
questions.a: In the repo next to the oracle, versioned, with a name that cites the incident.

attack-success-leakage-rates.explain:
## What it is

Report **attack-success rate (ASR)**, **sensitive-data leakage rate**, and **unsafe-action rate** with a sample size and a confidence note. **0/20 is not 0%.** It is 'fewer than about 15% at 95% if you must put a number', or better: publish k/n and keep running. Compare releases on the **same suite**. A lower ASR with a much higher false-positive rate on benign traffic may be a worse product.

Leakage rate is not the same as ASR: an attack can succeed at manipulation without leaking. Unsafe-action rate counts executor events, not model prose.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you talk to leadership and auditors. Interviewers will ding 'we are secure, zero successes' on a tiny n. On the job, these three rates plus false positives are the dashboard.

## How it works + one small example

Dashboard: ASR overall and by family (encoding, corpus, tool); leakage (canary appears); unsafe actions (policy-breaking tool calls); benign block rate. Release A 4% ASR vs B 2% but B blocks 10% more good asks — you do not ship B without a quality conversation.

Use the same seeds and n when you compare. Changing the suite and the model in one release confounds the number.

## Failure modes

1. **0/20 = 0%** in a slide.

2. **Changing the suite** and claiming a win.

3. **Ignoring benign blocks.**

4. **Counting model refusals as safe actions** when no tool was even attempted.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I report attack-success, leakage, and unsafe-action rates as k/n on a fixed suite, and I never call 0/20 zero risk. I compare releases on the same cases and I show the benign-block trade-off.

## A concrete walk-through

The board deck said '0% ASR'. You replace it with 0/40 and a planned n=200, plus a 3% benign-block. The conversation becomes adult.

## What I would measure

Suite version in every report; n; ASR vs benign-block; unsafe-action count in production (should match canaries).

## Interview follow-up

When the interviewer changes the constraints — half the latency budget, a new region, a hostile document, a cheaper model — I keep the same skeleton for Report **attack success rate (ASR)**, **sensitive data leakage rate**, and **uns and swap the binding constraint. The skeleton is: 1) Publish k/n, not a fake zero from a small n; 2) ASR, leakage, and unsafe-action are different; 3) Compare releases on the same suite; 4) Show false positives / benign blocks; 5) Unsafe-action is an executor event. The sentence I can say under pressure is: I report attack-success, leakage, and unsafe-action rates as k/n on a fixed suite, and I never call 0/20 zero risk. I compare releases on the same cases and I show the benign-block trade-off.

I do not restart from a blank architecture. That is what junior answers do. I show what I would drop first and what I would never drop.

## How this fails in a real review

This topic dies when it lives only in a prompt or a wiki page. Prompts regress on the next model bump; wiki pages do not run in CI. I put the control in code and the proof in a test. I also watch for correlated layers that look like depth and fail together.

## What I would do on Monday

I would pair with the owner of the executor, the retriever, or the gateway — whichever box this topic touches — and add the smallest check that would have caught last quarter's near-miss. Then I would re-run the relevant suite or eval and write the delta in the release notes.
keyPoints: Publish k/n, not a fake zero from a small n.
ASR, leakage, and unsafe-action are different.
Compare releases on the same suite.
Show false positives / benign blocks.
Unsafe-action is an executor event.
Do not confound a suite change with a model change.

questions.q: Why can 0 successes out of 20 attacks not be reported as 0% attack success?
questions.a: The interval is wide; a later attack or a model bump can land. Report 0/20 and keep testing, or compute a bound — do not say zero risk.

questions.q: Release A has ASR 4% and release B 2% on the same suite, but B also blocks 10% more benign requests. How do you decide?
questions.a: Treat it as a trade-off. If B's extra blocks are high-value tasks, it may be worse. Look at unsafe-action rate and user impact, not ASR alone.

questions.q: Why measure end-to-end attack success separately from model-only?
questions.a: A model may comply while the executor denies, or refuse while a renderer still leaks. The product number is end-to-end.

questions.q: What is an unsafe-action rate?
questions.a: The share of runs where a policy-breaking tool call was executed, not merely proposed. It is the number finance cares about.

questions.q: How do you keep a comparison fair?
questions.a: Pin the suite version, n, and environment. Change one thing per release note.

a-living-attack-suite.explain:
## What it is

**Each new jailbreak becomes a regression case.** The suite is not a PDF from last year. When a researcher publishes a new encoding, when your red team lands a novel path, when a customer reports a weird send, you add a fixture in the same sprint. Ownership is explicit: a rotation or a security engineer merges cases like product bugs.

Living also means retiring cases that no longer match the product (you removed the tool) and keeping the oracle current.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Static suites rot. Interviewers ask how a new public jailbreak enters your repo. On the job this is the difference between a one-off pentest and a practice.

## How it works + one small example

SLA: 5 business days from a notable public technique or an internal find to a draft case. Template: goal, payload, oracle, control. Weekly triage like a bug scrub.

If you removed `send`, you keep one case that asserts the tool is absent, and you archive the old send-exfil payloads so someone does not re-add the tool quietly.

## Failure modes

1. **Annual pentest only.**

2. **Cases in a slide deck.**

3. **Never deleting obsolete cases**, so CI is noise.

4. **No owner.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A living attack suite means each new jailbreak or incident becomes a case in days, with an owner, and obsolete cases are archived on purpose. A yearly PDF is not a suite.

## A concrete walk-through

A new paper drops on Monday. Wednesday a fixture is in review. Friday CI fails on staging because the renderer missed a scheme. That is living.

Time-to-case; cases closed as obsolete with an absence test; unowned open case count.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on **Each new jailbreak becomes a regression case.** The suite is not a PDF from la is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. The spoken close stays the same: A living attack suite means each new jailbreak or incident becomes a case in days, with an owner, and obsolete cases are archived on purpose. A yearly PDF is not a suite.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

Teams skip this when a demo is due. The skip shows up later as an incident, a surprise bill, or a questionnaire they cannot answer. I write the failure modes into the runbook so the next on-call does not rediscover them. I also refuse a change that cannot be tested, versioned, and rolled back.

## What I would do on Monday

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.

questions.a: On a stated SLA, typically days, as a draft case with an oracle. Do not wait for the annual test.

questions.q: You removed send_email. What happens to the old exfil cases?

questions.a: It is not executed, not mutated, and not blocking merges. It is a snapshot.

questions.a: Goal, payload, oracle, expected control, and a link to the incident or paper.

success-rate-not-anecdotes.explain:
## What it is

**Report how many of 50 attacks landed, with the control that stopped them.** Anecdotes ('we tried a jailbreak and it failed') are not a security posture. Fifty is a round classroom number; the point is a denominator and a per-control breakdown: 8/50 landed, 30/50 died on the allow-list, 10/50 died on the renderer, 2/50 died on the judge.

This item is the communication standard for the module. Pair it with the earlier warning that 0/20 is not zero.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Leadership and interviews both reward numbers with denominators. Anecdotes hide concentration: all failures in one family.

## How it works + one small example

A one-slide table: family × outcome × control. Speak: 'Of 50 corpus injections, 4 retrieved and 1 executed a tool; the allow-list stopped the rest of the executions. We will add hidden-text cases next because 3 of the 4 retrievals were comments.'

Do not average away the family. One number is a start; the table is the answer.

## Failure modes

1. **'The demo looked safe.'**

2. **One blended ASR** with no family.

3. **No control column**, so you do not know what to fund.

4. **n=3** presented as a study.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I report k of n attacks and which control stopped the rest — for example 4 of 50 landed, allow-list stopped most executions. Anecdotes are not a rate, and a blended percentage without families hides where to invest.

## A concrete walk-through

You replace a 'we red-teamed it' slide with a 50-case table. Budget moves from a new judge to the allow-list tests because that is what stopped 30 cases.

## What I would measure

Reports that include k/n and a control column; families with n too small to interpret.

## Interview follow-up

When the interviewer changes the constraints — half the latency budget, a new region, a hostile document, a cheaper model — I keep the same skeleton for **Report how many of 50 attacks landed, with the control that stopped them.** An and swap the binding constraint. The skeleton is: 1) Always give k/n, not a story; 2) Break down by family and by control that stopped it; 3) Fifty is a teaching n; the denominator is the point; 4) Anecdotes hide concentration of failures; 5) Fund the control that actually stops the mass of cases. The sentence I can say under pressure is: I report k of n attacks and which control stopped the rest — for example 4 of 50 landed, allow-list stopped most executions. Anecdotes are not a rate, and a blended percentage without families hides where to invest.

I do not restart from a blank architecture. That is what junior answers do. I show what I would drop first and what I would never drop.

This topic dies when it lives only in a prompt or a wiki page. Prompts regress on the next model bump; wiki pages do not run in CI. I put the control in code and the proof in a test. I also watch for correlated layers that look like depth and fail together.

## What I would do on Monday

I would pair with the owner of the executor, the retriever, or the gateway — whichever box this topic touches — and add the smallest check that would have caught last quarter's near-miss. Then I would re-run the relevant suite or eval and write the delta in the release notes.

Break down by family and by control that stopped it.
Fifty is a teaching n; the denominator is the point.
Anecdotes hide concentration of failures.

questions.q: What does a good red-team report include besides a narrative?
questions.a: k/n overall and per family, and which control stopped the failures. That tells you what to fund.

questions.q: Why not only quote a blended ASR?
questions.a: All the misses may be one family (hidden HTML). A blend looks 'fine' while that family is wide open.

questions.a: So you do not delete it in a refactor, and so you invest in the one doing the work rather than a favourite filter.

bias-transparency-human-oversight.explain:
## What it is

Core concerns around **hallucination, bias and fairness, transparency, accountability, and human oversight** are not slogans; they are design constraints. Hallucination is a wrong statement presented as fact. Bias is systematic error across groups (a resume screener that down-ranks a school or a name). Transparency is being able to say what the system does, on what data, with what limits. Accountability is a named owner when it hurts someone. Human oversight is a person who can change the outcome — not a rubber stamp.

**Automation bias** is the tendency of that person to believe the machine. Oversight that is a pre-checked 'agree' box is not oversight. High-stakes uses (hiring, credit, benefits, medical) need slower, documented, challengeable human decisions and measured error by group.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the ethics and governance core of the capstone. Interviewers will ask how you test a resume screener and whether 'a human reviews everything' is enough. On the job it is how you keep a feature from becoming a discrimination incident.

## How it works + one small example

Resume screener: define the decision (rank, not reject); measure selection rates and error by group on a labelled set; remove features that proxy protected attributes when you can; document remaining risk; a human must see the evidence, not only a score; log overrides. Transparency: a system card that says it ranks, it hallucinates citations unless grounded, it is not a legal decision.

Test automation bias: if reviewers agree with the model 99% in one second, the human is decoration. Change the UX: hide the score until they write a note, or sample mandatory disagreements.

## Failure modes

1. **'A human reviews'** with no time, no evidence, no override metric.

2. **No group-wise eval** because overall accuracy looked fine.

3. **Transparency as a marketing page** that disagrees with the code.

4. **Accountability with no name.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I treat hallucination, bias, transparency, accountability, and oversight as design constraints. I measure error by group, I document limits, I name an owner, and I do not call a one-second rubber stamp human oversight — automation bias is the failure mode.

## A concrete walk-through

You hide the score until the reviewer writes two bullets from the evidence. Override rate rises from 0.5% to 8%. That is oversight starting to exist. You add group-wise charts to the monthly review.

## What I would measure

Group-wise error; override rate and time; incidents with a named owner; mismatch between the system card and the code.

## Interview follow-up

## What it is

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

2. **No version.**

The cheap objection is that this is overkill for a prototype. A prototype can be smaller, but the constraint still belongs in writing so we do not promote the prototype unchanged. Another objection is that the next model will make the problem go away. A better model does not remove a missing ACL, a shared admin token, an unmeasured p95, or a cache key without a tenant. I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What I would do on Monday

I would add one test or one dashboard panel that makes this topic visible, name an owner in the design doc, and put the thirty-second line at the top of the PR. If I cannot name the owner and the metric, I do not understand the work yet. I would rather ship a smaller capability with a measured residual than a demo that fails the first red team or the first traffic spike.
